title: SR&ED Wages and Salaries - Canadian Tax Credit Glossary
description: Learn how to claim SR&ED Wages and Salaries in Canada with our R&D tax credit glossary covering eligible employee remuneration rules.
summary: In Canada, SR&ED wages and salaries paid to employees directly engaged in scientific research and experimental development are the primary expenditure driver for most claims. Bonuses, profit-based remuneration and taxable benefits are excluded from the 55% proxy salary base, and the salary of a specified employee included in that base is capped at the lesser of 75% of the employee's salary or wages for the year and 2.5 times YMPE.

Executive Legislative Overview and Statutory Architecture
Evolution of the Canadian R&D Tax Regime and the Bill C-15 Reforms

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, established in its modern statutory structure by the federal budget of May 23, 1985, serves as the cornerstone of Canada's national innovation policy and remains the single largest federal source of financial support for industrial research and development. Administered jointly through legislative design by the Department of Finance Canada and operational enforcement by the Compliance Programs Branch of the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the program incentivizes businesses of all sizes and industrial sectors to conduct systematic scientific and technological investigation within Canada. Unlike discretionary government grants that rely on competitive budget envelopes, ministerial pre-approvals, and fixed application windows, the SR&ED program operates as an entitlement-based statutory tax incentive embedded directly within the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), hereinafter the "ITA") and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, hereinafter the "ITR"). Provided a taxpayer satisfies the substantive scientific and technological criteria of subsection 248(1), adheres to the expenditure rules of sections 37 and 127, and files the prescribed reporting forms within the strict statutory deadline, the resulting income deductions and Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) vest as a matter of legal right.

Between 2012 and 2024, a series of federal legislative amendments progressively narrowed the generosity of the SR&ED regime by reducing the basic ITC rate from 20% to 15% after 2013, lowering the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) overhead rate from 65% to 60% for 2013 and to 55% for 2014 and later years, restricting arm's-length subcontractor and third-party payment inclusions to 80% after 2012, and eliminating capital expenditures and capital lease costs from SR&ED eligibility effective January 1, 2014. However, the enactment of Bill C-15, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, introduced the most expansive structural modernization of the SR&ED program in over three decades. Applicable retroactively to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024—and, with respect to depreciable capital property and capital lease costs, to property acquired or lease amounts that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024—the Bill C-15 reforms reversed key austerity measures from the 2012–2014 era and substantially broadened access to refundable tax credits for scaling domestic technology enterprises.

body.text: The policy architecture of Bill C-15 addresses three structural bottlenecks that historically penalized Canadian innovators as they scaled beyond early-stage venture financing. First, doubling the annual expenditure limit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 and widening the prior-year taxable capital phase-out band from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000 reflects a decade of wage inflation in scientific and engineering disciplines and prevents mid-sized domestic enterprises from prematurely losing access to the 35% refundable credit. Second, extending the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—and introducing an elective three-year average gross revenue phase-out test under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32)—eliminates the structural penalty whereby Canadian technology and life sciences firms previously forfeited refundable SR&ED status immediately upon listing on a public stock exchange or raising substantial balance-sheet equity that inflated their taxable capital employed in Canada. Third, reinstating capital expenditures for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, corrects a decade-long statutory bias toward pure software claimants by restoring tax support for hardware prototyping, advanced manufacturing, clean technology, lab instrumentation, and domestic high-performance computing infrastructure.
Dual Statutory Mechanism Under Sections 37 and 127 of the Income Tax Act

The federal SR&ED incentive operates through a two-stage statutory mechanism that separates the income tax deduction of research expenditures from the generation of investment tax credits. Understanding the precise statutory interaction between these two stages is critical for accurate corporate tax provisioning, audit defence, and multi-year financial modelling.

The first stage is governed by section 37 of the ITA, which establishes a dedicated tax expenditure pool for SR&ED carried on in Canada, alongside limited permissible SR&ED carried on outside Canada under subsections 37(1.5) and 37(2). Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may pool all qualifying current SR&ED expenditures—and, for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, eligible capital SR&ED expenditures—incurred in the taxation year. Rather than capitalizing these research costs or amortizing them under standard Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) classes, the taxpayer may deduct any portion of the section 37 SR&ED expenditure pool in computing net business income for the current taxation year, or carry the undeducted balance forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. This indefinite deduction carryforward is particularly advantageous for pre-profit enterprises that wish to preserve ordinary non-capital loss carryforwards (which expire after 20 taxation years) or manage current-year taxable income to stay beneath provincial small-business or R&D phase-out thresholds.

The second stage is governed by sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA, which calculate the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) based on the taxpayer's "qualified expenditure" pool defined in subsection 127(9). While the section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool largely overlap, they diverge in two vital respects. Where a taxpayer elects to use the Proxy Method under ITR subsection 2900(4), the Prescribed Proxy Amount (equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base) is added solely to the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool for the purpose of generating ITCs; because the PPA is a notional statutory calculation rather than an actual cash outlay, it is never deductible under section 37. Conversely, eligible payments to arm's-length Canadian subcontractors and eligible third-party payments are 100% deductible in the section 37 expenditure pool, whereas only 80% of such contract expenditures qualify for inclusion in the subsection 127(9) pool for ITC calculation.

Furthermore, to prevent double-dipping between the full deduction of expenses under section 37 and the receipt of tax credits under section 127, paragraph 37(1)(e) and paragraph 12(1)(t) of the ITA mandate a recapture into taxable income of any federal SR&ED ITC claimed or refunded. Specifically, any federal SR&ED ITC applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable or refunded in cash in a given taxation year reduces the taxpayer's section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year; if that reduction exceeds the available balance in the section 37 pool, the negative balance is included directly in the taxpayer's business income under paragraph 12(1)(t) in that subsequent taxation year. By contrast, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits—such as the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit, the Quebec CRIC, the British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit, and the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant—constitute "government assistance" under subsections 127(9) and 127(18), which reduces both the section 37 deductible pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool in the current taxation year in which the assistance is received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received.
Scientific and Technological Eligibility Under Subsection 248(1)
Statutory Categories of Eligible Work and Excluded Activities

Eligibility for the SR&ED program does not depend on the commercial success of a product, the industrial sector of the claimant, or the novelty of a business model; rather, it turns strictly on whether the underlying activities satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The statute subdivides qualifying investigation into three primary research categories alongside a fourth category of eligible support work.

The first category, basic research under paragraph (a) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1), encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, which typically occurs in academic partnerships, fundamental biotechnology, or theoretical materials science. The second category, applied research under paragraph (b), comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. The third and predominant category, experimental development under paragraph (c), covers work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto; in Canadian administrative practice, the vast majority of industrial SR&ED claims are filed as experimental development. The fourth category, commensurate support work under paragraph (d), captures work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Simultaneously, paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) expressly exclude specific commercial, routine, and non-technological activities from qualifying as SR&ED, even when performed inside an R&D-intensive company. These statutory exclusions encompass market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.

A critical analytical distinction arises in audit practice between excluded routine engineering or routine computer programming and eligible paragraph (d) support work. Standard software development, system configuration, user interface design, API integration, or routine debugging performed on a standalone commercial product is ineligible because it relies on standard procedures known to competent professionals. However, once a valid technological uncertainty and an experimental development core are established under paragraph (c), the computer programming, engineering design, mathematical analysis, data collection, and testing activities that are commensurate with the needs and directly in support of resolving that technological uncertainty become fully eligible under paragraph (d) until the technological uncertainty is resolved and commercial production begins.
Judicial Interpretation and the Five Criteria of Northwest Hydraulic

Because subsection 248(1) is drafted in concise statutory language, Canadian tax jurisprudence has played the decisive role in operationalizing the legal boundary between eligible experimental development and ineligible routine engineering. The foundational judicial authority in Canadian tax law is the May 1, 1998 decision of Justice Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, Docket 97-531-IT-G, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), which examined five hydraulic engineering projects. The principles articulated in Northwest Hydraulic were subsequently adopted and elevated to binding appellate precedent by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA), and CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (affirming 2000 DTC 2372 (TCC)).

Under the Northwest Hydraulic and CW Agencies legal test, a taxpayer bears the burden of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that each claimed project satisfies five cumulative criteria, universally referred to in CRA audit manuals and Tax Court jurisprudence as the "Five Questions":

headers: The Five Judicial Criteria (Northwest Hydraulic / CW Agencies)
Core Legal and Technical Threshold Required by the Courts

cells: Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?

The uncertainty must exist in the underlying science or technology, not merely in commercial viability, cost, or project scheduling. If the resolution of the problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures or routine engineering known to competent professionals in the field, no technological uncertainty exists. Uncertainty may arise from a system-level constraint where known components interact in an unpredictable manner.
Hypothesis Formulation: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?

The claimant must follow a five-stage cognitive progression: observation of the subject matter, identification of the technological uncertainty, formulation of a causal hypothesis proposing how to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty, testing of the hypothesis by experiment or analysis, and modification or substantiation of the hypothesis based on empirical results. Unstructured trial-and-error without causal hypotheses fails this test.
Systematic Investigation (Scientific Method): Did the procedures adopted accord with the established and objective principles of the scientific method?

The investigation must be characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, or rigorous mathematical and engineering analysis, directed by qualified personnel at the cutting edge of the technology. Ad hoc troubleshooting, intuition-driven coding, or unmeasured parameter tweaking does not constitute a systematic investigation.
Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advancement?

The work must generate new technological knowledge or advance the general understanding of technology to a competent professional in the field. Crucially, the rejection or falsification of a hypothesis is itself a technological advancement if it systematically eliminates a plausible avenue of investigation and proves why a given technical approach cannot work under specified constraints.
Contemporaneous Documentation: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results kept as the work progressed?

As Justice Bowman stated in Northwest Hydraulic, "It seems self-evident that a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests and results be kept, and that it be kept as the work progresses". Contemporaneous records are treated by the courts as a natural by-product of the scientific method and essential corroboration of oral testimony.

body.text: Evolution of Case Law and the Tension Between CRA Administrative Policy and Jurisprudence

Subsequent decisions of the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal have refined the application of the Northwest Hydraulic criteria across software, food processing, civil engineering, and industrial manufacturing sectors, exposing critical compliance traps for claimants. In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, Justice D'Arcy dismissed the taxpayer's appeal in its entirety despite acknowledging that the company had maintained thorough documentation demonstrating a systematic engineering approach. The court held that satisfying Criterion 3 (systematic investigation) and Criterion 5 (contemporaneous documentation) cannot salvage a claim that fails Criterion 1: because the mechanical design challenges faced by Jentel were resolvable through routine engineering and standard practice by skilled personnel, no underlying technological uncertainty existed. Similarly, in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (affirming 2020 TCC 47, where the Tax Court judge found that the taxpayer failed four of the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria; leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed with costs on March 9, 2023, SCC File No. 40303), the courts disallowed claims where the taxpayer asserted high-level product objectives without proving that standard industry techniques were inadequate or without producing empirical test logs tied to specific causal hypotheses. By contrast, in Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108, Chief Justice Rossiter allowed the taxpayer's appeal and found that the claimed projects qualified as SR&ED. Additional recent Tax Court rulings involving roller-compacted concrete, fish processing projects exceeding $1.8 million across five taxation years, and railway engineering further illustrate how the courts dissect multi-component projects—for example, allowing SR&ED credits for a Safety Integrity Level 4 (SIL-4) train control system where genuine algorithmic and hardware uncertainties were articulated, while simultaneously rejecting an adjacent SCADA monitoring framework that relied on established industry engineering knowledge.

Conversely, the Tax Court of Canada's decision in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 159 (Informal Procedure), provides an essential judicial counterbalance in favour of taxpayers on three recurring audit disputes. In Manning Canning, the appellant undertook experimentation to control microbial growth and develop a vinegar-based beverage that would remain shelf-stable at room temperature. The Minister of National Revenue denied the claim on the grounds that the taxpayer experimented with chemical preservatives—potassium sorbate, sodium benzoate, and ultimately Chiber—that were already publicly known to competent food scientists, had allegedly failed to conduct a systematic investigation, and had not kept academic-grade records. Justice Bodie overturned the Minister's denial and allowed the appeal on all five Northwest Hydraulic questions.

First, Manning Canning establishes that a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty can exist even where a publicly available solution or chemical agent is known in general literature, provided that the solution has never been applied or proven to work within the claimant's specific technical context and constraints. Second, Justice Bodie clarified the legal standard for Criterion 5 (contemporaneous documentation), holding that contemporaneous records are meant simply to track the hypotheses generated, the experiments undertaken to test those hypotheses, and the results obtained as the work progressed; documentation does not need to be formatted or written so that an outside third party unfamiliar with the specific field of science or technology could replicate the experiments. Third, Manning Canning resolved the tension between jurisprudence and the CRA's administrative "How and Why" methodology. Although the CRA restructured its eligibility guidance around two administrative requirements ("Why" the work was conducted to achieve a technological advancement, and "How" the work was conducted via a systematic investigation) derived from subsection 248(1), Justice Bodie confirmed that the five questions established in Northwest Hydraulic remain a fully valid and authoritative legal methodology in the Tax Court of Canada.
Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and Refundability Rules
Enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit for CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations

Under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(10.1) of the ITA, Canada operates a two-tiered federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit rate structure. The premier incentive is the enhanced 35% ITC rate, which consists of the 15% basic ITC rate under subsection 127(9) combined with an additional 20% ITC rate provided under subsection 127(10.1) on a qualifying corporation's qualified SR&ED expenditures up to its annual "expenditure limit".

Prior to the enactment of Bill C-15, subsection 127(10.1) restricted the 35% enhanced rate exclusively to corporations that were, throughout the taxation year, Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) as defined in subsection 125(7) of the ITA. To qualify as a CCPC under subsection 125(7), a corporation must be a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation and must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (de jure or de facto control), by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), by a corporation with a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange, or by any combination thereof. Under the pre-reform law, if a Canadian startup raised a majority financing round from foreign venture capital investors or completed an initial public offering on a designated stock exchange, its CCPC status terminated immediately, causing its federal SR&ED rate to drop from a 35% refundable credit to a 15% non-refundable credit.

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, Bill C-15 amended subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(10.1) to extend the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) throughout the taxation year. Under the statutory definition in subsection 127(9), an ECPC is a corporation that, throughout the taxation year, is resident in Canada, has a class of shares of its capital stock listed on a designated stock exchange (or has elected in prescribed manner to be a public corporation), and is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. This legislative amendment ensures that domestically controlled public companies enjoy full parity with CCPCs in accessing the 35% refundable credit on up to $6,000,000 of annual qualified SR&ED expenditures.
Expenditure Limit Formula, Capital Phase-Out, and the Three-Year Gross Revenue Election

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit for qualifying CCPCs under subsection 127(10.2) and for ECPCs under subsection 127(10.6) is $6,000,000, doubled from the $3,000,000 limit applicable to taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024. At the 35% enhanced rate, a $6,000,000 expenditure limit yields a maximum federal refundable ITC of $2,100,000 per year, compared to $1,050,000 under the legacy provision.

Under subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA, a CCPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis when the taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and any associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000 (expanded from the legacy phase-out range of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000). The exact statutory formula in subsection 127(10.2) is:

where variable A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise equals the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada over $15,000,000.

Every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1. Crucially, tax auditors and corporate advisers must verify that prior-year taxable income does not enter the federal subsection 127(10.2) formula. While prior-year taxable income between $500,000 and $800,000 historically reduced the federal expenditure limit prior to 2019, the 2019 federal budget implementation legislation amended subsection 127(10.2) to permanently remove taxable income as a factor in determining a corporation's federal expenditure limit. Consequently, a highly profitable CCPC with $20,000,000 in prior-year taxable income but $15,000,000 or less in prior-year taxable capital retains the full $6,000,000 federal expenditure limit.

body.text: To address the reality that public corporations and venture-backed deep-tech CCPCs frequently hold substantial equity reserves or debt facilities on their balance sheets (which inflate taxable capital) while generating minimal commercial revenue during multi-year R&D cycles, Bill C-15 introduced a three-year average annual gross revenue phase-out mechanism. For an ECPC under subsection 127(10.6)—or a consolidated ECPC group under subsection 127(10.61) and subsection 127(10.62), defined by reference to "consolidated financial statements" in subsection 233.8(1)—the expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 based on the corporation's or consolidated group's average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years, rather than taxable capital. Simultaneously, subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) permit a single CCPC or an associated group of CCPCs to formally elect for a taxation year to have its expenditure limit determined under the ECPC three-year average gross revenue formula instead of the subsection 127(10.2) taxable capital formula. Where a CCPC or associated CCPC group files this election, the taxable capital phase-out under subsection 127(10.2) does not apply for that taxation year. For asset-heavy but low-revenue biotechnology, semiconductor, clean-energy, or hardware CCPCs whose prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000 due to equity or debt financings, electing under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32) preserves up to the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit.

Specific statutory rules also govern associated corporate groups, amalgamations, and short taxation years. Under subsection 127(10.21), associated CCPCs share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit, and the expenditure limit of every associated corporation is deemed to be nil unless the group files an allocation agreement in prescribed form (T2 Schedule 49) under subsection 127(10.3) assigning the shared limit among the associated members, failing which the Minister may allocate the limit under subsection 127(10.4). Subsections 127(10.22), 127(10.23), 127.1(2.2), and 127.1(2.3) further regulate deemed non-association and refundable ITC entitlements among associated CCPCs. Where a corporation is formed by amalgamation, paragraph 87(2)(j.6) provides continuity rules deeming the new corporation to be a continuation of each predecessor corporation for purposes including subsection 127(10.2). Finally, under subsection 127(10.5) (renumbered from former subsection 127(10.6) by Bill C-15) and subsection 127(10.64), a corporation with a short taxation year of less than 51 weeks must prorate its expenditure limit under paragraph 127(10.5)(b) by multiplying the limit by the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365, and special allocation rules apply where an associated CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year.
Basic 15% Investment Tax Credit, Refundability Tiers, and Carryover Mechanics

Qualified SR&ED expenditures that do not qualify for the 35% enhanced rate—including expenditures of a CCPC or ECPC in excess of its annual expenditure limit, as well as all qualified expenditures of foreign-controlled corporations, non-qualifying public corporations, individuals, and trusts—earn the basic federal ITC rate of 15% under subsection 127(9).

Whether an earned SR&ED ITC is paid out as a direct cash refund or must be applied strictly to offset Part I federal income tax payable is governed by the "refundable investment tax credit" provisions in section 127.1 (including subsections 127.1(2), 127.1(2.01), and 127.1(2.2)) of the ITA. Any SR&ED ITC refunded in the taxation year is deemed to be an ITC applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in the year.

body.text: Because a partnership is not a taxpayer under the ITA, SR&ED ITC amounts are calculated at the partner level and allocated to eligible members (excluding "specified members" who are passive or limited partners, and excluding certain trusts with tax-exempt or Crown corporation beneficiaries under provincial parallels). For any portion of an SR&ED ITC that is non-refundable or remains unclaimed after current-year tax offsets and refunds, subsection 127(5) and subsection 127(9) permit the unused ITC balance to be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years to reduce Part I federal income tax payable.
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures and Methodological Elections
Traditional Overhead Method Versus the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount

To compute its qualified SR&ED expenditures for a taxation year, a taxpayer must elect on Form T661 between two mutually exclusive accounting methodologies for capturing overhead and indirect supporting expenditures: the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method. Once a method is elected in the filed Form T661 for a given taxation year, that election is irrevocable for that year, although the taxpayer may elect differently in subsequent taxation years.

Under the Traditional Method, the taxpayer must specifically identify, track, and substantiate each individual overhead expenditure that is directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—meaning the expense would not have been incurred but for the SR&ED work. While the Traditional Method can benefit facility-intensive industrial or manufacturing claims where incremental shop supplies and utilities exceed 55% of direct research wages, it imposes a demanding financial audit burden because every overhead invoice must be proven to be directly attributable and incremental to the SR&ED project.

Consequently, the overwhelming majority of Canadian SR&ED claimants elect the Proxy Method under ITR subsection 2900(4). Under the Proxy Method, instead of claiming specific overhead expenses, the taxpayer calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of its eligible SR&ED salary base for the taxation year. Auditors and practitioners must strictly enforce the 55% PPA rate under ITR subsection 2900(4), as the historical 65% rate has not been in force since 2012.
Salaries, Wages, and Statutory Restrictions on Specified Employees

Salaries and wages paid to employees who are directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada constitute the primary expenditure driver for most claims. However, the ITA and ITR impose strict statutory exclusions and caps on eligible salaries, particularly with respect to the PPA salary base under ITR subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) and Specified Employees (employees who do not deal at arm's length with the employer or who own, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation).

body.text: As established under ITR subsections 2900(7) to 2900(9), the salary base to which the 55% PPA applies is substantially narrower than total payroll: bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits are excluded for all employees, and for a specified employee the PPA salary base is capped at the lesser of 75% of the employee's salary or wages for the year and 2.5 times the year's maximum pensionable earnings. Furthermore, founder-shareholders who draw compensation through dividends rather than T4 employment salary cannot include those dividends in SR&ED salaries.
Materials Consumed or Transformed and Subcontractor Inclusion Rules

Direct materials used in SR&ED qualify as eligible expenditures when they are either materials consumed (rendered virtually valueless or destroyed during experimental trials) or materials transformed (integrated into a prototype or experimental construct) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Where a claimant engages arm's-length Canadian subcontractors or makes third-party payments for SR&ED carried out in Canada on its behalf, 100% of the expenditure is deductible under section 37, but only 80% of the eligible contract payment is included in qualified expenditures for ITC calculation under subsection 127(9) (a restriction in force since after 2012). In audit practice, a claimant's contract payments will be denied by the CRA if the written agreement between the contracting parties fails to properly evidence the intention that the SR&ED work be performed on behalf of the claimant. For non-arm's length transactions and transfers of property or services, subsections 127(11.6) to 127(11.8) and subsection 127(33) apply specific look-through cost rules and anti-avoidance adjustments.
Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs Post-December 15, 2024

After an eleven-year exclusion that began on January 1, 2014, Bill C-15 amended section 37 and subsections 127(9), 127(11.2), 127(11.5), 127(11.8), 127(33), and 127.1(2.01) of the ITA to restore SR&ED eligibility for capital expenditures and capital lease costs. Under these transitional rules, depreciable property qualifies only if it is acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (subject to the timing-of-acquisition rules in subsection 127(11.2)), and lease costs qualify only with respect to lease amounts that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024. Any capital equipment acquired between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, remains permanently excluded from federal and provincial SR&ED capital claims.

To qualify under the restored rules, the depreciable capital property must be used all or substantially all—defined as 90% or more—for SR&ED in Canada over its useful life. Consequently, mixed-use machinery that splits its operating time between commercial manufacturing and experimental development and falls short of the 90% SR&ED utilization threshold is wholly ineligible. Furthermore, the statute expressly excludes buildings, land, inventory, and goodwill from qualifying as SR&ED capital expenditures under any circumstances. When eligible capital property is claimed by a qualifying CCPC or ECPC within its $6,000,000 expenditure limit, it earns the 35% enhanced ITC rate, but the resulting credit is refundable up to 40% under subsection 127.1(2.01) (producing an immediate 14% cash refund and a 21% non-refundable tax offset). If capital property included in a claim is subsequently disposed of or converted to commercial use, statutory recapture rules reverse the previously claimed federal and provincial credits.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentive Regimes

Every Canadian province (with the exception of Prince Edward Island) and the Yukon Territory operates a provincial or territorial R&D tax incentive that stacks atop the federal SR&ED program. While provincial regimes rely on the federal definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, significant structural divergences have emerged between "follower" provinces that aligned with the federal Bill C-15 reforms (such as British Columbia) and "holdout" or independently reformed jurisdictions (such as Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba, and Alberta).

body.text: Ontario R&D Tax Incentives: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Ontario drives more than half of Canada's total SR&ED claims and operates three distinct R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), S.O. 2007, c. 11, Sched. A, and Ontario Regulation 37/09, all administered by the CRA since January 1, 2009.

The primary SME incentive is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) under section 96 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), claimed on T2 Schedule 566. The OITC provides a flat 8% refundable tax credit (reduced from 10% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016) on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000, yielding a maximum refundable credit of $240,000 per year. Crucially, Ontario has not adopted the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit or expanded OITC eligibility to public corporations; the $3,000,000 Ontario expenditure limit remains separate from the $6,000,000 federal limit and is restricted exclusively to CCPCs. Furthermore, the $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit is shared among associated corporations and is phased out on a straight-line basis when the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or when its prior-year specified/taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Where both thresholds are exceeded in the preceding taxation year, the two reduction ratios combine multiplicatively rather than by taking the lesser of the two separate limits:

headers: Prior-Year Taxable Capital in Canada (Associated Group)

body.text: Alongside the OITC, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on T2 Schedule 508, provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016) available to all corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario with no expenditure cap, a 3-year carryback, and a 20-year carryforward. Additionally, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit up to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap for SR&ED performed under contract with an eligible Ontario research institute, such as a university, college, or approved hospital research organization. While older text on the provincial website continued to state that capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013, were ineligible, Ontario's 2026 Fall Economic Statement annex confirmed that capital expenditures for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (used 90% or more for SR&ED in Ontario) are restored as eligible expenditures for both the OITC and the ORDTC, providing an estimated $50 million in additional tax support over three years for roughly 700 businesses (with a 23.56% recapture rate applicable to the ORDTC upon subsequent disposition or commercial conversion).

When calculating the statutory interaction among the OITC, the ORDTC, and the federal SR&ED ITC, CRA policy (Section 4.5.4 and Appendix A of the Assistance and Contract Payments Policy) and Ontario law establish a strict ordering rule. Although some secondary commentary mistakenly suggests reducing the OITC base by the federal ITC or ORDTC, the CRA's authoritative provincial policy confirms that qualified expenditures for the OITC are reduced by external government and non-government assistance, but are NOT reduced by the OITC, the OBRITC, the ORDTC, or the federal SR&ED ITC. Conversely, the OITC is expressly treated as government assistance for ORDTC purposes and reduces the Ontario expenditure pool on which the 3.5% ORDTC is calculated. Thus, on $1,000,000 of eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures, a qualifying CCPC earns an $80,000 OITC ($1,000,000 × 8%) and a $32,200 ORDTC (($1,000,000 − $80,000) × 3.5%), for combined Ontario credits of $112,200 (11.22% of the eligible pool). Both Ontario credits then reduce the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure pool under ITA subsection 127(18), unless the corporation delivers a formal written waiver of the OITC or ORDTC with its return on or before six months after its taxation year-end (or on an amended return).
Quebec R&D Tax Reform: Transition from Legacy Wage Credits to the Unified CRIC Regime

Quebec administers its R&D tax incentives independently through Revenu Québec and requires claimants to file Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures) alongside the applicable tax credit form. Following the Quebec Budget 2025–2026, Quebec executed a sweeping structural transition for taxation years and partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025.

For taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning on or before March 25, 2025, claimants remain under the legacy four-credit regime described in Revenu Québec document IN-109-V (Tax Assistance for Scientific Research and Experimental Development): the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7-V), the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V, requiring a qualification certificate issued by the Minister of Economy, Innovation and Energy), and the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V).

For taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, the four legacy credits cannot be claimed, Form RD-1029.7-V is barred and rejected, and claimants must transition to the new Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC), claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR. To qualify under the CRIC regime, a corporation or qualified partnership must carry on business in Quebec, maintain an establishment in Quebec, and incur expenditures in respect of R&D or pre-commercialization activities carried out in Quebec by it or on its behalf under contract. Crucially, CRIC expands eligible expenditure categories beyond traditional R&D wages to encompass salaries and wages, consideration paid to subcontractors, payments to eligible research organizations, and capital expenditures for the acquisition of property used in R&D or pre-commercialization activities (while repealing separate legacy industrial design credits). While the maximum Quebec R&D credit rate reaches 30% on eligible spending, the CRIC tax credit rate for a corporation that is a member of a qualified partnership is set at 20% (reported on lines 440p to 440y, codes 112 and 113, of Guide CO-17.G).
Alberta Innovation Employment Grant and Incremental Base-Level Mechanics

Enacted effective January 1, 2021, under sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and detailed in Alberta Corporate Income Tax Information Circular IEG-1, the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) is delivered directly through the Alberta corporate tax system under the lead policy oversight of the Ministry of Technology and Innovation. Corporations claim the IEG by filing AT1 Schedule 29 (Form A29) and Form AT4970 (Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Claimed in Alberta) with their Alberta corporate income tax return on or before 15 months after the corporation's filing-due date.

The IEG provides benefits on up to $4,000,000 in annual eligible R&D spending carried out in Alberta (matching the expenditures that qualify for the federal SR&ED program, where the expenditure limit is allocated under section 127(10.2) of the federal ITA) through a two-tier incremental structure:

items: Base Payment (8% Rate): Qualified corporations receive an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base level of spending, where the base level is calculated as the corporation's average qualifying R&D spending over the preceding 2 taxation years.

Enhanced Incremental Payment (20% Rate): Qualified corporations receive an additional 12% benefit—producing an enhanced 20% refundable payment—on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's two-year historical base spending level, up to the $4,000,000 annual expenditure cap.

body.text: To target small and medium-sized enterprises, the IEG phases out incrementally for corporations (and associated groups) with between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital, and corporations with $50,000,000 or more in taxable capital are ineligible. While eligible expenditures for the IEG are reduced by external government and non-government assistance (other than the IEG and the federal SR&ED ITC), any Alberta IEG received reduces the federal pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and federal qualified SR&ED expenditures, and any subsequent property conversion or disposition triggers Alberta tax recapture.
British Columbia and Manitoba R&D Tax Credit Regimes

British Columbia offers a 10% SR&ED tax credit (BCITC) and is the premier example of express provincial alignment with the federal Bill C-15 reforms. Following the federal changes, British Columbia extended access to its 10% refundable provincial credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), restored capital expenditures as qualifying B.C. SR&ED expenditures, and increased its prior-year taxable capital phase-out range to $15,000,000 to $75,000,000. (Technical Audit Note: In corporate tax software and T2 filings, practitioners must never confuse the BC SR&ED credit with T2 Schedule 422 / Form T1196, which is the British Columbia Film and Television Tax Credit).

In Manitoba, the Manitoba Research and Development Tax Credit equals 15% of eligible expenditures made after April 11, 2017 (reduced from the pre-April 12, 2017 rate of 20%). For in-house R&D, one-half (50%) of the credit—an effective rate of 7.5%—is refundable, and the remaining 50% (7.5%) is non-refundable. Because Manitoba does not utilize the federal enhanced-credit expenditure limit, the federal increase to $6,000,000 does not create a corresponding new limit in Manitoba.
Government Assistance Grinding, Grant Stacking, and Multi-Jurisdictional Modelling
Statutory Reduction Rules Under Subsections 127(18) to 127(21)

Under subsections 127(11.1) and 127(18) to 127(21) of the ITA, a taxpayer's qualified SR&ED expenditures must be reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payment that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of the SR&ED. As illustrated in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, even conditionally repayable government contributions—where periodic repayments depend on future product revenues reaching a specified threshold and terminate on a fixed date regardless of whether the full principal has been repaid—constitute government assistance that reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures immediately under subsection 127(18). Furthermore, where government assistance received on a specific project exceeds that project's qualified expenditures, subsections 127(19), 127(20), and 127(21) mandate that the excess assistance be applied to reduce other qualified SR&ED expenditures of the corporation or of associated corporations.
Strategic Stacking with NRC IRAP, Mitacs, OIDMTC, and Export Grants

By strategically combining non-dilutive federal and provincial grants with SR&ED and provincial tax credits, Canadian technology and manufacturing companies routinely achieve 51% to 75%+ cost recovery on their innovation budgets. Each funding layer interacts differently with the subsection 127(18) assistance grind:

body.text: In executing these multi-layer stacks, claimants must strictly segregate cost pools so that the same labour dollar is never double-claimed across mutually exclusive provincial incentives—such as separating interactive digital media labour claimed under the uncapped 40% Ontario Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit (OIDMTC) from technological uncertainty labour claimed under SR&ED and IRAP. Similarly, sector-specific Ontario programs such as the Ontario Vehicle Innovation Network (OVIN, offering up to $1,000,000 for automotive and mobility R&D) and the Ontario Centre of Innovation Critical Industrial Technologies (OCI CIT) streams—Future Ready ($10,000), Talent Development Internships ($20,000 per SME), Development and Commercialization ($100,000), and Sector Adoption ($1,000,000 at a 33% cost-share)—layer directly onto the SR&ED-OITC-IRAP foundation while reducing the net SR&ED expenditure base only by the portion of grant funding directly attributable to SR&ED-eligible tasks.
Administrative Compliance, Filing Procedures, and CRA Audit Defence
Mandatory Tax Forms and the Strict 18-Month Statutory Filing Bar

To claim federal SR&ED deductions and Investment Tax Credits, a taxpayer must prepare and submit prescribed forms with its annual income tax return. Corporations must file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) together with T2 Schedule 31 (T2SCH31) (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations), while unincorporated individuals file Form T661 alongside Form T2038-IND (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)). Associated CCPCs must also file T2 Schedule 49 to allocate the shared expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.3), and provincial claimants must enclose the corresponding provincial schedules, such as T2 Schedule 566 (OITC) and T2 Schedule 508 (ORDTC) in Ontario, AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970 in Alberta, or Form RD-222-V and Form RD-1029.8.CR in Quebec.

The most critical procedural compliance requirement in Canadian R&D tax law is the strict 18-month reporting deadline codified in subsection 37(11) (for SR&ED expenditure deductions) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (for SR&ED ITCs). Under paragraph 150(1)(a) of the ITA, a corporation's T2 income tax return is due within 6 months after the end of its taxation year. Subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) allow an additional 12 months beyond the T2 filing-due date to submit the prescribed SR&ED forms and prescribed information, establishing an absolute filing window of 18 months from the end of the taxation year (and 15 months after the AT1 filing-due date for the Alberta IEG). Crucially, there is no statutory mechanism or ministerial discretion to extend the 18-month federal or Ontario SR&ED filing deadline; any claim filed past the 18-month bar is permanently disallowed by operation of law.
CRA Technical and Financial Review Workflows

As detailed in the CRA's SR&ED Technical Review: A Guide for Claimants and the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors, every SR&ED claim is initially assessed for risk at the CRA Tax Centre upon filing. If the CRA is satisfied with the validity and low risk profile of the submission, the claim is Accepted as Filed (AAF) without further audit intervention. Claims that are not accepted as filed are forwarded to a Coordinating Tax Services Office (TSO), where the Control Centre determines whether the claim will undergo a desk review or a detailed technical and financial audit conducted by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), a Financial Reviewer (FR), or both.
When a claim is selected for detailed review, the audit workflow follows a rigorous administrative sequence:

headers: Key Procedural Actions and Claimant Rights

cells: Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) & Financial Reviewer (FR) at TSO

RTA and FR review the current Form T661, prior claim history, and financial schedules; if not accepted as AAF after desk review, the CRA notifies the claimant by phone or letter and issues a formal Request for Information (RFI) letter.

A list of activities and documents to be examined is sent in advance; the RTA interviews technical staff to assess the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria. At the end of the site visit, the RTA must give the claimant a preliminary verbal indication of eligibility decisions or outstanding concerns so the claimant can submit additional representations.
The RTA documents technical eligibility findings in an SR&ED Review Report provided to the claimant, and the FR works with the RTA to issue a joint CRA Proposal Letter.
Research & Technology Manager (RTM), Financial Review Manager (FRM), & Assistant Director, SR&ED

Before a reassessment is finalized, the claimant is encouraged to resolve disagreements first with the RTA/FR, second with the RTM or FRM, and third by requesting an Administrative Second Review by the Assistant Director, SR&ED.
If the claimant disagrees with the final Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the first formal dispute step is filing a Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch.
Tax Court of Canada & Department of Justice (DOJ) Counsel

If the Notice of Objection is unsuccessful, the claimant uploads a Notice of Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada (which serves the CRA); the DOJ files a written Reply within 60 days of service; the claimant may file an Answer within 30 days of the Reply, closing the pleadings stage before discovery and trial.

body.text: Contemporaneous Documentation Standards, Objections, and Tax Court Appeals

Under section 5.6.6.2 of the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors—quoting Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839—the CRA strictly enforces the rule that "Oral statements are not a substitute for the claimant keeping adequate documentation or other evidence". While oral testimony from the engineers and scientists who performed the work is considered during site visits and Tax Court hearings, the CRA will deny SR&ED expenditures where a claimant cannot produce contemporaneous documentation generated during the implementation of the project. To satisfy both the RTA and the FR, claimants should maintain project planning documents, documents on the design of experiments, dated records of hypotheses, test logs, and empirical results kept as the work progressed, alongside clear asset-allocation notes linking post-December 15, 2024 capital equipment to specific SR&ED projects and properly worded written subcontractor contracts.
Strategic Conclusions and Compliance Governance

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026 (retroactive to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024) and Quebec's implementation of the CRIC regime (for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025) represent a generational expansion of Canadian R&D tax incentives. To capture these enhanced statutory benefits while maintaining audit readiness before the CRA and Revenu Québec, corporate tax executives and engineering leaders should execute four core compliance actions.

First, domestic public companies that qualify as Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) under subsection 127(9) should immediately transition their tax provisioning to claim the 35% refundable federal ITC (and the aligned 10% refundable British Columbia credit, where applicable) on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures, while capital-intensive CCPCs whose prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000 should model the subsection 127(10.31) / 127(10.32) election to use three-year average gross revenue in order to preserve their enhanced 35% expenditure limit. Second, businesses acquiring laboratory instrumentation, hardware test benches, or dedicated AI compute infrastructure on or after December 16, 2024, should isolate those assets from commercial production and maintain contemporaneous utilization logs demonstrating 90% or greater SR&ED use over the asset's expected useful life to secure the restored federal, Ontario, British Columbia, and Quebec capital tax credits. Third, multi-jurisdictional filers must respect provincial divergences by accounting for Ontario's unaligned $3,000,000 OITC cap and multiplicative taxable income/capital grinds on T2 Schedule 566, evaluating whether to waive the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC when in a tax-loss position, and retiring legacy Quebec Form RD-1029.7-V in favour of Form RD-1029.8.CR (CRIC) for all taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. Finally, claimants should embed the five judicial criteria of Northwest Hydraulic and the contextual documentation standards of Manning Canning directly into their daily engineering and project-management workflows, ensuring that every SR&ED claim is backed by contemporaneous evidence of technological uncertainty, causal hypothesis testing, and systematic investigation filed strictly within the non-extendable 18-month statutory deadline.
